Knife forums inevitably have posts that start out with "I found this ______, what should I do with it?". It's a natural question, and a good answer can be the thing that starts someone down the path of both collecting and using knives.

This post isn't designed to get into the identification of your knife. That is a science and skill all in itself (especially with vintage knives). This post is designed to inform you the options you have available to you when presented with a knife.

the first option, and one that should be used on any potentially valuable, family heirloom type knife is to PRESERVE it in it's existing condition. All that discoloration on the blades, the wear marks, the blade with the bit of the tip missing... those are what we call patina, and it's presence can (and does) add provenance and value to a knife. Serious collectors would rather have an old Case or S.C.C. with a cracked handle, a tipped blade or maybe even a missing blade than one some monkey with a sander tried to make shiny again.

That being said, "Dirt Ain't Patina" and doesn't add anything. To clean a vintage knife (either to preserve it, or to assess it's condition) use the following:

  • Mineral oil/soft cloth - Cleans off surface grime, residue and things of that nature. Can't hurt anything on the knife and will do wonders for stacked leather handles. Elbow Grease only, no power anything.
  • You can use a wooden toothpick to get down into backsprings and pivots, the wood is soft enough that it won't scratch or damage the knife. Great at getting "gunk" out of a recess.
  • Compressed Air - Self explanitory. Once you dislodge gunk, you gotta get it out of the knife. Mineral Oil and Air through a pivot is a great way to remove old grit and rust particles that build up when I knife has been stored without oil in the pivot.

Once you have a clean specimen, you need to determine if you want to PRESERVE it. If you do:

  • I highly recommend Renaissance Wax. It's a microcrystalline wax designed for use on nearly all materials by the British Museum. It will protect surfaces from the everyday "rigors" of a knife that sits in a display case or safe.
  • I have also heard (but not personally used) Walker Wax is a fine product. Collectors I regard highly swear by it. The application of either is the same. Rub on, wipe off with a soft cloth.

If you have decided that Preservation isn't' enough, and you need to do some CLEANING or RESTORATION, the following list is a progression of suggestions from least destructive, to the most:

  • Pencil lead - Take a #2 pencil and heavily color on the active rust (the red or orange stuff). The lead is soft enough to remove some of the rust and not damage the steel itself. Wipe it down with Mineral oil when done. May take a few passes.

  • Flitz (or Simichrome) and a soft cloth - Removes tarnish, some surface patina and discoloration. These are very mild abrasives, they won't do much to the steel, but can be detrimental to handle materials

  • Rust Eraser â€“ Abrasive.Come in a number of â€œgritsâ€ (use the finest grit that works for you) these are usually silicon carbide grit embedded in a rubber block. They will â€œscrubâ€ off patina and light rust. They will change how the finish of your blade looks.

  • Steel wool - Abrasive. Will remove discoloration and some mild surface corrosion. This WILL change how the finish of the blade looks. Some people like how steel wool finishes, I for one don't. It looks like amateur hour.

  • 3M ScotchBrite pad (fine) - A woven abrasive. Will remove surface corrosion and discoloration. Changes now the blade finish looks. If you do it correctly (i.e. run it down the blade all the same direction, back to front) and you're careful about getting it right up tight against the guard, this will look decent.

  • Automotive sandpaper - Used in progressively finer grits (start with 400, 600, 800, 1000, 1500, 2000) you can remove just about any surface problem. Use a hard backed sanding block so you don't round off the grind lines. Like with the 3M stuff, sand only in one direction so you're not imparting random scratches to the surface. Some people go to 800 and decide they like the "handrubbed" look. If you go all the way to 2000, then you use something like Simichrome or flitz, it'll look decent. You can buy Micromesh abrasives all the way up to 12000 grit.

Any method you choose, it's all about taking your time and being consistent. No power tools, please. Dremel tools are notoriously difficult to use to get anything resembling a decent polished finish, power sanders will ruin the blade temper faster than you can react, and the buffer is hands down the most dangerous tool you could use in a shop (as in, could, and has killed even professional knifemakers, See the tragic case of Gordon Dempsey).

That all being said, if you're not familiar or comfortable working on something, then there's no shame in seeking professional help with it. There are some people out there that are willing to take on restoration jobs, but you need to have a firm understanding of what these folk's time is worth to them. You can spend more on a professional restoration than the value of the knife to begin with.

Also remember that anytime you do anything to a knife, aside from preserve it, you change the value, many times not for the better.
